title: Lose your life to find it
plain: Jesus says that people who try to hang on to their lives will lose them, and people who let go of their lives for his sake will find them. It sounds like nonsense if 'life' means the same thing both times. The saying works because it plays on two meanings of life: the self we grip and protect, and the deeper life God gives.
takeaway: The life you grip shrinks; the life you hand over to God comes back larger.

poleA.label: Lose your life
poleA.statement: Following Jesus means denying yourself, taking up a cross and being willing to lose your life.

poleB.label: Find your life
poleB.statement: The one who loses life for Jesus' sake will find it, keep it and gain eternal life; Jesus came so people would have life abundantly.

tension: If the goal is life, why is the path loss? And if loss is the path, is Christianity simply a call to self-hatred? The saying seems to make the same thing both the price and the prize.

resolutions.name: Two senses of 'life'
resolutions.heldBy: Most commentators across traditions
resolutions.explanation: The Greek word *psyche* can mean physical life, the self, or the whole person. Jesus contrasts the self-protective life (security, status, comfort as the final goal) with the life that comes from God. Holding the first as ultimate costs you the second.

resolutions.name: Martyrdom and resurrection
resolutions.heldBy: Early church readers, many Catholic and Orthodox writers, and scholars focused on the original setting
resolutions.explanation: In the first setting the cross was literal: some disciples would actually die. The promise is that death for Christ is not the end, because God raises the dead. The saying is first about physical death and future resurrection, and only then about everyday self-denial.

resolutions.name: Daily dying to self
resolutions.heldBy: Monastic, Pietist, Wesleyan and many evangelical devotional traditions
resolutions.explanation: Luke adds 'daily': the cross is a habit of putting God and neighbour ahead of self-will. The 'finding' is experienced now as freedom from the anxious project of self-protection, not only after death.

resolutions.name: Seed logic
resolutions.heldBy: Johannine readers; Augustine and many preachers
resolutions.explanation: John frames it with a grain of wheat: it must fall into the ground and die to bear fruit. The loss is real but it is the loss of a seed, not of a stone. The pattern is first Jesus' own death and resurrection, then the disciple's.

skeptic.objection: This is a manipulative contradiction: it tells people to give up their lives and calls that gaining them, which can be used to justify abuse, burnout or needless martyrdom.
skeptic.reply: The saying is a paradox, not a contradiction, because 'life' is used in two senses. It is also qualified: the loss is 'for my sake and the gospel's', not for any leader's convenience. The same Jesus warns against loading burdens on others and rebukes leaders who lord it over people. Christians have sometimes misused the text, but the text itself sets love of God and neighbour, not self-destruction, as the goal.

practical: Ask where you are gripping: reputation, money, control, safety. Letting go there is not losing yourself but making room for God. It does not mean neglecting your health or accepting mistreatment; Jesus withdrew to rest and avoided danger when his time had not come (Mark 6:31, John 7:1).

title: Strength made perfect in weakness
plain: Paul asked God three times to take away a painful 'thorn in the flesh'. God said no, telling him that grace was enough and that divine power is made perfect in weakness. So Paul says, 'when I am weak, then I am strong'.
takeaway: Weakness is not the opposite of God's power; it is often where that power shows most clearly.

poleA.label: I am weak
poleA.statement: Paul is genuinely weak: afflicted, insulted, in hardships and distress, carrying treasure in a clay jar.

poleB.label: I am strong
poleB.statement: In that very weakness Christ's power rests on him, so that he can say he is strong.

tension: Strength and weakness seem to exclude each other. If God is powerful, why not simply remove the weakness? And does praising weakness make Christianity passive or resigned?

resolutions.name: Power that is not ours
resolutions.heldBy: Reformed and Lutheran theology (Luther's 'theology of the cross')
resolutions.explanation: Human weakness removes the illusion that results come from our ability. When strength remains obviously God's, God gets the credit and we stop trusting ourselves. The clay jar shows that the power belongs to God.

resolutions.name: Cross-shaped pattern
resolutions.heldBy: Many New Testament scholars (e.g. those stressing 'cruciformity') and Catholic and Orthodox spirituality
resolutions.explanation: Jesus was 'crucified in weakness' yet lives by God's power. The apostle shares that pattern. Weakness is not a malfunction but the shape of Christ's own path from cross to resurrection.

resolutions.name: Grace sufficient in the moment
resolutions.heldBy: Pastoral and devotional readings broadly
resolutions.explanation: The promise is not that weakness disappears but that grace is enough for each moment. The strength is endurance, courage and fruitfulness inside the limits, not escape from them.

resolutions.name: Paul's polemical point
resolutions.heldBy: Historical-critical readers of 2 Corinthians
resolutions.explanation: Paul is answering rival 'super-apostles' who boasted of impressive gifts and presence. By boasting in weakness he redefines what counts as apostolic credentials. The paradox is partly rhetoric aimed at a specific church dispute, though it states a lasting principle.

skeptic.objection: Saying weakness is strength is a way of explaining away unanswered prayer: if God helps, he is strong; if he doesn't, weakness is 'strength'. The claim can't lose.
skeptic.reply: Paul admits the prayer was refused and the pain stayed. He does not deny weakness; he claims something else happened through it: endurance and effective ministry that he attributes to God. Whether one accepts that attribution is a matter of faith, but the claim is not empty: Paul lists concrete sufferings and concrete outcomes. Christians also pray for healing elsewhere in the New Testament (Jas 5:14-15), so the text does not teach that God never removes weakness.

practical: Name a limitation honestly instead of hiding it. Pray for it to be removed, as Paul did, and also ask what God might do through it if it stays. Communities can learn to value people whose weakness is visible rather than only the polished and gifted.

title: The first will be last
plain: Jesus repeatedly says that many who are first will be last and the last first. He says it after Peter asks what the disciples will get for leaving everything, and in a parable where late workers are paid the same as early ones. It reverses the normal ranking of who matters.
takeaway: God's kingdom does not follow our pecking order, and those who assume they are at the front should be careful.

poleA.label: The first
poleA.statement: Some are first now: early, established, religious insiders, the rich and secure.

poleB.label: The last
poleB.statement: The last will be first: latecomers, outsiders, the poor and those with no claim are welcomed and raised.

tension: Does this mean ranks are simply flipped, so the poor are now on top? Or that there are no ranks at all? And isn't paying latecomers the same unfair to those who worked all day?

resolutions.name: Grace erases merit ranking
resolutions.heldBy: Protestant and many Catholic interpreters of the vineyard parable
resolutions.explanation: In the parable everyone gets a full day's wage. The point is not a new hierarchy but that the reward is a gift, so nobody can rank themselves above others. The grumbling of the early workers is the real target.

resolutions.name: Eschatological reversal
resolutions.heldBy: Scholars stressing Jesus as a prophet of God's coming reign; liberation theologians
resolutions.explanation: When God's kingdom fully comes, present status will be overturned: the humble lifted, the proud brought down. This echoes Mary's song and Jesus' beatitudes and woes. The reversal is real and future-facing, a warning to the comfortable and hope for the overlooked.

resolutions.name: Israel and the nations
resolutions.heldBy: Some historical readings (e.g. in Luke 13 context)
resolutions.explanation: In Luke 13 the saying follows people coming from east and west to the feast while some insiders are shut out. One application is that Gentiles, late to the covenant, are welcomed alongside or ahead of many in Israel who rejected Jesus.

resolutions.name: Warning to disciples
resolutions.heldBy: Many pastoral readings
resolutions.explanation: In Matthew 19-20 it is aimed at Peter and the Twelve. Even those who left everything must not assume they are first; seeking position is the very attitude the kingdom overturns.

skeptic.objection: The vineyard owner is unjust: equal pay for unequal work. A just God would reward people in proportion.
skeptic.reply: No one in the parable is cheated: the early workers get exactly the wage they agreed. The latecomers get generosity, not justice. The story asks whether we can bear God being generous to others. Readers can still debate whether grace and desert should be kept apart this sharply; the New Testament elsewhere speaks of rewards matched to faithfulness (1 Cor 3:12-15), so many hold both together.

practical: Notice who you quietly rank below you at church or work. Celebrate the newcomer's welcome instead of measuring it against your own service.

title: The greatest is the servant
plain: When the disciples argued about who was greatest, Jesus told them that whoever wants to be great must be the servant of all. He pointed to himself: he came not to be served but to serve and give his life. Leadership in his community is measured by service, not by status.
takeaway: In Jesus' kingdom, greatness is not climbing up but stooping down.

poleA.label: Greatness
poleA.statement: Jesus does not forbid wanting to be great; he speaks of the greatest and the first, and the apostles will sit on thrones.

poleB.label: Servanthood
poleB.statement: The great must be a servant (*diakonos*) and the first a slave of all, following Jesus who washed feet and gave his life.

tension: Is servanthood the path to greatness (a means), or is it what greatness actually is? And how does this fit with real authority in the church?

resolutions.name: Greatness redefined
resolutions.heldBy: Most commentators
resolutions.explanation: Jesus contrasts Gentile rulers who 'lord it over' others. He does not abolish greatness but redefines it: the measure of greatness is how much one serves. Service is not a stepping stone to some other kind of status; it is the status.

resolutions.name: Servant authority
resolutions.heldBy: Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant ecclesiologies (the pope's title 'servant of the servants of God' reflects this)
resolutions.explanation: Real offices and authority exist in the church, but they are held as service. Elders are to shepherd willingly and not domineer. Authority is legitimate when used for others' good.

resolutions.name: Exaltation follows humility
resolutions.heldBy: Many readings of Philippians 2 and the wisdom tradition
resolutions.explanation: There is a sequence: humble yourself and God will exalt you. Christ's own path went from servant form to the cross to being exalted. The reward is real but it is God's to give, not something grabbed.

resolutions.name: Anti-hierarchy reading
resolutions.heldBy: Some Anabaptist, Quaker and egalitarian readers
resolutions.explanation: Jesus' words undercut ranked offices altogether: 'you are all brothers' and you should not be called rabbi or father. The church should be as flat as possible, with roles but not ranks.

skeptic.objection: Churches preach servant leadership while building powerful hierarchies, so the saying is either ignored or used as a cover for control.
skeptic.reply: The objection is a fair criticism of practice, and the text itself supports it: Jesus aims these words precisely at leaders who seek status. But hypocrisy in following a teaching is not a contradiction in the teaching. Traditions differ on how much structure the saying allows, which is a genuine debate rather than a settled point.

practical: If you lead, ask who your decisions actually serve. If you don't, notice that greatness in Jesus' terms is available to anyone willing to do unseen work for others.

title: Rich yet poor, poor yet rich
plain: Paul says Jesus was rich but became poor so that through his poverty believers might become rich. The church is called poor yet making many rich, having nothing yet possessing everything. At the same time Revelation warns a wealthy church that it is actually poor.
takeaway: Real wealth is measured by what you have in God, and Jesus became poor to share it.

poleA.label: Poor
poleA.statement: Christ emptied himself and became poor; his people are often poor, and God chooses the poor of this world.

poleB.label: Rich
poleB.statement: Through his poverty believers become rich; the poor church in Smyrna is called rich; they possess all things.

tension: Is this riches in money or only 'spiritual' riches? If only spiritual, is it a consolation that keeps the poor quiet? If material, why are so many believers poor?

resolutions.name: The great exchange (incarnation)
resolutions.heldBy: Church Fathers broadly (e.g. Gregory of Nazianzus on Christ's self-emptying) and most traditions
resolutions.explanation: The eternal Son set aside the glory and privileges he had and entered human poverty and death, so that humans might share in his life and inheritance. The riches are union with God and a share in Christ's inheritance.

resolutions.name: Spiritual wealth now, full inheritance later
resolutions.heldBy: Many evangelical and Catholic readings
resolutions.explanation: Believers can be materially poor and yet rich in faith, forgiveness and hope, with an inheritance kept in heaven. Revelation's Laodicea shows the reverse: materially rich, spiritually poor.

resolutions.name: Economic sharing in the body
resolutions.heldBy: Scholars noting the context of 2 Corinthians 8 (the collection); liberation and Anabaptist readers
resolutions.explanation: Paul cites Christ's poverty to urge the Corinthians to give money to poor believers in Jerusalem 'so that there may be equality'. The paradox has a concrete economic edge: the rich become 'poorer' by sharing so the poor are lifted.

resolutions.name: Prosperity reading
resolutions.heldBy: Word of Faith and prosperity teachers
resolutions.explanation: Christ became poor so that believers can become financially rich now. Critics from almost every other tradition respond that the context is generosity toward the poor, and that Paul himself was often hungry and in need.

skeptic.objection: Calling poor people 'rich' is just religion as an opiate: it redescribes poverty instead of fixing it.
skeptic.reply: That critique (associated with Marx) has force against some preaching. But in its context, 2 Corinthians 8 is a fund-raising letter for the material relief of the poor, and James condemns rich people who exploit workers (Jas 5:1-6). The New Testament keeps both: spiritual riches that do not depend on money, and a demand that those with money share it.

practical: Let the paradox work in both directions: be content and grateful if you have little, and generous if you have much. Give in a way that costs something, following the shape of Christ's own giving.

title: Dying, and behold we live
plain: In 2 Corinthians 6 Paul strings together contrasts: treated as impostors yet true, unknown yet well known, dying and yet alive, sorrowful yet always rejoicing. He describes believers as carrying Jesus' death in their bodies so that Jesus' life shows. Death and life run through the Christian at the same time.
takeaway: The Christian life holds real dying and real living together, because it follows Jesus' death and resurrection.

poleA.label: Dying
poleA.statement: Believers are always being given over to death, have died with Christ, and face real suffering and mortality.

poleB.label: Living
poleB.statement: Yet they live; the life of Jesus is shown in their mortal flesh, and they have been raised with Christ.

tension: How can someone be both dying and living? Is the dying literal persecution, inward self-denial, or both? Is the life now or only after death?

resolutions.name: Union with Christ
resolutions.heldBy: Pauline scholars and most traditions
resolutions.explanation: Paul sees believers as joined to Christ, sharing his death and resurrection. Baptism enacts this. Because they are 'in Christ', both his dying and his rising are true of them at once.

resolutions.name: Outer and inner self
resolutions.heldBy: Common pastoral reading
resolutions.explanation: The outer person, the body, is wasting away under hardship and age, while the inner person is renewed day by day. The two statements apply to different aspects of the same person.

resolutions.name: Already and not yet
resolutions.heldBy: Many New Testament theologians
resolutions.explanation: Resurrection life has begun through the Spirit but bodily resurrection is still future. Believers live in the overlap of the old age, which is passing away, and the new, which has broken in.

resolutions.name: Apostolic hardship catalogue
resolutions.heldBy: Historical readings of 2 Corinthians
resolutions.explanation: Paul is answering critics who thought his beatings and poverty disqualified him. He turns the list of sufferings into evidence that he follows a crucified and risen Lord. The 'dying' is first his literal near-deaths.

skeptic.objection: 'Dying yet living' is just poetic spin to make suffering sound meaningful.
skeptic.reply: It is poetic, and Paul knows it. But it rests on a factual claim he stakes everything on: that Jesus was raised (1 Cor 15:14-19). If that is false, Paul himself says Christians are to be pitied. So the paradox is not spin detached from claims; it stands or falls with the resurrection.

practical: When you face loss, illness or opposition, the paradox gives permission to name the dying honestly while looking for signs of life: endurance, love, hope. Neither pretend all is well nor assume all is lost.

title: Free, yet slaves
plain: Paul says he is free from everyone yet has made himself a slave to all. He also says believers were set free from sin and became slaves of righteousness and of God. Christian freedom is not having no master but having the right one.
takeaway: Freedom in the Bible is freedom from what destroys you for the sake of love that serves.

poleA.label: Free
poleA.statement: Christ has set believers free; they are not to submit again to a yoke of slavery; the truth makes them free.

poleB.label: Slaves
poleB.statement: Believers are slaves of righteousness and of God, and they are to serve one another in love.

tension: If believers are free, why describe them as slaves? And if they are slaves, in what sense are they free? Modern readers also hear 'slave' with painful historical weight.

resolutions.name: Everyone serves something
resolutions.heldBy: Augustine and most Western theology; Paul's own argument in Romans 6
resolutions.explanation: Paul assumes no one is truly masterless: you serve sin or you serve God. Freedom is being released from a master that leads to death to one that leads to life. True freedom is the ability to become what you were made for.

resolutions.name: Luther's double thesis
resolutions.heldBy: Lutheran tradition (Luther, *The Freedom of a Christian*, 1520)
resolutions.explanation: Luther stated it as two propositions: a Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none, and a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all. Free by faith before God; servant by love toward the neighbour.

resolutions.name: Freedom used for others
resolutions.heldBy: Pastoral readings of 1 Corinthians 9
resolutions.explanation: Paul's freedom is real, but he gives up rights (to pay, to food, to customs) so as to win others. Chosen self-limitation is an exercise of freedom, not a loss of it.

resolutions.name: Social-historical reading
resolutions.heldBy: Scholars of Roman slavery and the New Testament
resolutions.explanation: In the Roman world being the slave of a powerful master could carry status, and 'slave of God' echoes Israel's prophets and kings called 'servant of the LORD'. Paul uses a familiar institution as a metaphor; he admits he speaks 'in human terms' because of their weakness.

skeptic.objection: Calling slavery freedom is Orwellian double-speak, and Christian slave language was used to keep real slaves obedient.
skeptic.reply: The history of misuse is real and should be faced honestly. But Paul's point is that humans are already bound to forces they did not choose, and that the gospel frees them from those. He also told enslaved believers to gain freedom if they could (1 Cor 7:21) and called Philemon to receive Onesimus as a brother. Many abolitionists drew on these texts. The metaphor's limits are worth naming, but it is a claim about whom we serve, not an endorsement of human ownership.

practical: Ask what actually controls you: approval, appetite, fear, money. Freedom starts there. Then ask how you can use your freedom for someone else's good rather than to insist on your rights.

title: The foolishness of God is wiser than men
plain: Paul admits that a crucified Messiah looks foolish to Greeks and offensive to Jews. Yet he says this 'foolish' message is God's power and wisdom. God's foolishness is wiser than human wisdom, and God's weakness stronger than human strength.
takeaway: The cross turns upside down what people assume wisdom and power look like.

poleA.label: Foolishness
poleA.statement: The message of the cross is foolishness to those perishing; God chose what is foolish in the world.

poleB.label: Wisdom
poleB.statement: To those being saved it is the power of God; Christ is God's wisdom; Paul speaks a hidden wisdom among the mature.

tension: Is Paul against reason and learning? If the gospel is 'foolish', why does Paul argue so carefully? And does this make faith immune to criticism?

resolutions.name: Against worldly wisdom, not against thinking
resolutions.heldBy: Most mainstream interpreters; Christian intellectual traditions (Augustine, Aquinas, Reformers)
resolutions.explanation: Paul targets the Corinthian love of eloquence and status-seeking philosophy, not reason itself. He reasons constantly. The wisdom he rejects is the kind that would never have imagined God saving through a cross.

resolutions.name: Revelation exceeds reason
resolutions.heldBy: Many Reformed, Lutheran and Orthodox writers
resolutions.explanation: Human reason could not discover the gospel unaided; it had to be revealed by the Spirit. Once revealed, it makes deep sense, but only from inside the new perspective it creates.

resolutions.name: Fideist reading
resolutions.heldBy: Some strands of Christian thought (often linked, with debate, to Tertullian and Kierkegaard)
resolutions.explanation: Faith embraces what reason finds absurd; that is its glory. Critics within the church reply that this misreads Paul, who appeals to evidence like resurrection witnesses (1 Cor 15:3-8).

resolutions.name: Social reversal
resolutions.heldBy: Social-scientific scholars of Corinth
resolutions.explanation: Most Corinthian believers were not wise, powerful or of noble birth. The paradox dismantles a status system that ranked people by education and rhetoric. God's choice of the low-status is itself the 'foolishness'.

skeptic.objection: Calling your belief 'God's foolishness' is a convenient way to dodge rational criticism: if it sounds silly, that proves it's true.
skeptic.reply: Paul does not say anything foolish is therefore true. He says one specific event, a crucified and risen Messiah, defied expectations, and he grounds it in public claims (eyewitnesses of the resurrection). The paradox describes why the message was offensive, not a rule that absurdity equals truth. Whether the claims hold up is open to examination, and Christian apologists and critics both engage it.

practical: Do not be ashamed of a faith that looks unimpressive, but also do not use 'foolishness' as an excuse for lazy thinking. Measure wisdom by love and humility, not by cleverness.

title: Answer a fool, do not answer a fool
plain: Two verses in a row in Proverbs give opposite commands: do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you will be like him; answer a fool according to his folly, or he will think himself wise. The collectors put them side by side on purpose. Wisdom is knowing which situation you are in.
takeaway: Proverbs are not rules for every case; wisdom means reading the situation.

poleA.label: Do not answer
poleA.statement: Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you also be like him.

poleB.label: Do answer
poleB.statement: Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes.

tension: Placed back to back, these look like a plain contradiction. Which instruction should a reader follow?

resolutions.name: Deliberate juxtaposition
resolutions.heldBy: Nearly all commentators, Jewish and Christian
resolutions.explanation: The editors were not careless: they placed these together to teach that proverbs are situational. The reasons given differ (protecting yourself vs correcting the fool), showing when each applies.

resolutions.name: Two ways of 'according to his folly'
resolutions.heldBy: Rabbinic discussion (Talmud, *Shabbat* 30b) and many later commentators
resolutions.explanation: The Talmud records that some sages wanted to hide Proverbs because of this tension, and resolved it by saying one verse concerns matters of Torah and the other worldly matters. Others say: do not stoop to the fool's methods (insults, rage), but do expose the fool's argument on its own terms.

resolutions.name: Silence as the default
resolutions.heldBy: Some wisdom and monastic traditions
resolutions.explanation: Proverbs elsewhere praises restraint of speech and warns against arguing with scoffers. Answer only when the fool's self-deception or influence on others makes silence harmful.

resolutions.name: Jesus as example of both
resolutions.heldBy: Christian preaching
resolutions.explanation: Jesus sometimes refused to answer (before Herod and Pilate) and sometimes answered trick questions in a way that exposed the questioners. He shows both verses in practice.

skeptic.objection: Here the Bible contradicts itself in consecutive verses; it cannot be a coherent guide.
skeptic.reply: A contradiction is two claims that cannot both be true in the same sense at the same time. These are instructions with different stated purposes, and everyday wisdom works the same way ('look before you leap' and 'he who hesitates is lost'). Because the verses are adjacent, the editors clearly saw the tension and meant it. If anything, it shows that the authors did not view Proverbs as a mechanical rulebook.

practical: Before replying online or in a heated argument, ask: will answering pull me down to their level, or will silence let a harmful falsehood stand? Then choose.

title: Judge not, yet judge rightly
plain: 'Judge not, that you be not judged' is one of the best-known lines Jesus said. Yet Jesus also says to judge with right judgment, and Paul tells the church to judge those inside it. So the Bible both forbids and commands judging.
takeaway: The Bible forbids hypocritical, condemning judgment but requires honest, humble discernment.

poleA.label: Do not judge
poleA.statement: Do not judge or you will be judged; remove the log from your own eye; who are you to judge your neighbour?

poleB.label: Judge rightly
poleB.statement: Do not judge by appearances but judge with right judgment; are you not to judge those inside the church?

tension: If judging is forbidden, how can the church discipline, discern false prophets or call sin sin? If it is commanded, what does 'judge not' actually rule out?

resolutions.name: Hypocrisy vs discernment
resolutions.heldBy: Most interpreters across traditions
resolutions.explanation: Matthew 7 targets the hypocrite who condemns a speck while ignoring a log. The same passage requires discernment: don't give holy things to dogs, beware false prophets, you will know them by their fruits. The log comes out so you can 'see clearly' to help.

resolutions.name: Condemnation belongs to God
resolutions.heldBy: Many Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant moral theologians
resolutions.explanation: Humans may assess actions but must not pronounce final verdicts on a person's heart or eternal destiny. Paul refuses to judge even himself before the Lord comes.

resolutions.name: Insiders and outsiders
resolutions.heldBy: Readings of 1 Corinthians 5
resolutions.explanation: Paul distinguishes: the church should not judge outsiders, whom God judges, but should hold its own members accountable. The command to judge applies to the community's internal life, aimed at restoration.

resolutions.name: Same measure
resolutions.heldBy: Pastoral readings
resolutions.explanation: Jesus does not say 'never evaluate' but 'the measure you use will be used on you'. Judge only with the mercy and standards you would accept for yourself.

skeptic.objection: The Bible says 'judge not' and then commands judging; Christians quote whichever suits them.
skeptic.reply: Selective quoting certainly happens. But the texts use 'judge' in different senses: condemning or passing final sentence versus assessing truth and behaviour. Matthew 7 itself contains both, within a few verses. The coherent picture is: assess carefully, start with yourself, aim to restore, and leave final verdicts to God.

practical: Before calling out someone else, look honestly at your own log. When correction is needed, do it privately first, gently, aiming at restoration. Refuse to pronounce on anyone's final standing with God.

title: Let your light shine, yet do good in secret
plain: In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus says to let your light shine before others so they see your good works. A few paragraphs later he says not to practise your righteousness before others to be seen by them, and to give in secret. Both are in the same sermon.
takeaway: The issue is not whether good works are seen but who gets the glory.

poleA.label: Be seen
poleA.statement: Let your light shine before others, so that they see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven.

poleB.label: Be hidden
poleB.statement: Beware of practising righteousness before others to be seen; give, pray and fast in secret.

tension: Should good works be public or hidden? It looks as if Jesus says both in the same sermon.

resolutions.name: Motive and goal
resolutions.heldBy: Most commentators (Chrysostom and Augustine discuss this)
resolutions.explanation: The difference is the purpose clause: 'so that they glorify your Father' versus 'to be seen by them'. Show your works when it points to God; hide them when showing would feed your own reputation.

resolutions.name: Different kinds of acts
resolutions.heldBy: Some interpreters
resolutions.explanation: Matthew 6 deals with religious practices (giving, prayer, fasting) that can be staged for applause. Matthew 5 is about a whole way of life in community, which cannot be hidden, like a city on a hill.

resolutions.name: Default to secrecy
resolutions.heldBy: Many monastic and devotional writers
resolutions.explanation: Because the heart easily craves applause, err on the side of hiddenness; the light will still shine through a life without being advertised.

resolutions.name: Witness as mission
resolutions.heldBy: Missional and evangelical readers
resolutions.explanation: Christian community is meant to be visible so that outsiders are drawn to God. Hiding good deeds out of false modesty can be its own failure.

skeptic.objection: Jesus contradicts himself within one sermon: show your good works, hide your good works.
skeptic.reply: A speaker who said both within minutes probably saw no contradiction. Each command carries its own purpose: one for God's glory, the other against self-promotion. The common thread is that the observer you care about should be God, whether or not people also see.

practical: Before posting or mentioning something good you did, ask whom it serves. Do some good things that no one will ever know about, to keep your motives honest.

title: Bear one another's burdens, bear your own load
plain: In Galatians 6 Paul says 'bear one another's burdens' and three verses later 'each will have to bear his own load'. In English it can look like a flat contradiction. Paul uses two different Greek words and two different situations.
takeaway: Help carry what crushes others, but do not hand off what is yours to carry.

poleA.label: Carry each other's
poleA.statement: Bear one another's burdens and so fulfil the law of Christ; restore the one caught in sin gently.

poleB.label: Carry your own
poleB.statement: Let each test his own work; each will have to bear his own load.

tension: Are Christians meant to share burdens or to carry their own? Does responsibility for others conflict with personal responsibility?

resolutions.name: Two different words
resolutions.heldBy: Most commentators
resolutions.explanation: Verse 2 uses *baros*, a heavy, crushing weight. Verse 5 uses *phortion*, an ordinary pack or load one is expected to carry (the same word Jesus uses for his light burden in Matt 11:30). Help with the crushing weights; carry your own daily pack.

resolutions.name: Present help, future accountability
resolutions.heldBy: Many commentators reading the future tense in v. 5
resolutions.explanation: Verse 5 may look ahead to final judgment: each person will answer for their own work before God. That does not cancel present mutual help; it warns against comparing yourself with others.

resolutions.name: Interdependence, not dependence
resolutions.heldBy: Pastoral and counselling applications
resolutions.explanation: Healthy community helps people in crisis but does not encourage someone to offload responsibilities they can carry. Paul also says those unwilling to work should not eat.

skeptic.objection: Galatians 6:2 and 6:5 plainly contradict each other three verses apart.
skeptic.reply: In English they sound alike, but in Greek Paul uses different words with different weights, and the surrounding verses explain each: verse 2 is about restoring someone overtaken by sin, verse 5 about not boasting by comparing yourself to others. Writing them so close together suggests Paul saw them as complementary.

practical: When a friend is overwhelmed, step in. When you are tempted to let others carry what you can manage, pick up your own pack. And stop measuring your load against other people's.

title: Hate your father and mother, honour your father and mother
plain: Jesus says that anyone who comes to him and does not hate father and mother cannot be his disciple. Yet the Ten Commandments say to honour father and mother, and Jesus himself condemned people who used religion to dodge caring for their parents. Both sayings are in the Bible and Jesus affirms both.
takeaway: Jesus demands first place, not literal hatred; love of family must not outrank love of God.

poleA.label: Hate them
poleA.statement: If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, he cannot be my disciple.

poleB.label: Honour them
poleB.statement: Honour your father and your mother; Jesus rebukes those who nullify this command by religious loopholes.

tension: How can Jesus command hatred of parents while upholding the command to honour them and himself caring for his mother from the cross?

resolutions.name: Semitic idiom of preference
resolutions.heldBy: Most scholars and commentators across traditions
resolutions.explanation: In Hebrew idiom 'love and hate' can mean 'prefer and put second'. Jacob 'loved Rachel more than Leah' and Leah is then called 'hated'; God 'loved Jacob and hated Esau'. Matthew's parallel says 'whoever loves father or mother more than me', which shows the sense.

resolutions.name: Shock language for a costly call
resolutions.heldBy: Many commentators
resolutions.explanation: The idiom explains the meaning but should not soften the force. In a society where family was everything, following Jesus could mean rejection by one's family. The strong word prepares disciples for that real cost.

resolutions.name: Rightly ordered love
resolutions.heldBy: Augustine's *ordo amoris* and much Catholic and Protestant ethics
resolutions.explanation: Love for family is good, but disordered if placed above God. When God is first, family love is not lost but put in its proper place, and becomes healthier.

skeptic.objection: Jesus commands hatred of family, contradicting both the Ten Commandments and his own teaching on love; this shows cult-like demands.
skeptic.reply: The objection takes 'hate' in its modern emotional sense. Matthew's version of the same saying ('loves more than me') and other Hebrew uses of the idiom point to priority, not hostility. Jesus also enforces care for parents (Mark 7:10-13) and provides for his mother as he dies. The saying does make an absolute claim on loyalty, and readers must judge whether such a claim is justified; but it is not a contradiction once the idiom is understood.

practical: Love your family wholeheartedly, and also notice where the desire to please family is shaping your choices more than God is. Following Christ should never be an excuse to neglect parents in need.

title: Be angry, and do not sin
plain: Paul quotes Psalm 4: 'Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger.' Yet a few verses later he says to put away all anger, and Jesus warns that anger with a brother is liable to judgment. Jesus himself was angry at hard hearts.
takeaway: Anger is not automatically sin, but it is dangerous, and it must be handled quickly.

poleA.label: Be angry
poleA.statement: Some anger is permitted, even right: Jesus was angry at hardness of heart and drove traders from the temple.

poleB.label: Put away anger
poleB.statement: Let all bitterness, wrath and anger be put away; the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.

tension: Is anger allowed or forbidden? Can a person be angry without sinning when Scripture also says to put away all anger?

resolutions.name: Righteous vs sinful anger
resolutions.heldBy: Most Christian ethics (Aquinas discusses anger that follows reason)
resolutions.explanation: Anger at real injustice, aimed at setting things right, can reflect God's own anger at evil. Anger that is selfish, vengeful or nursed into bitterness is sin. Eph 4:31 targets the latter.

resolutions.name: Concession with a time limit
resolutions.heldBy: Many commentators
resolutions.explanation: The Greek imperative may function as a concession: 'If you are angry, don't sin.' The emphasis falls on the limit: settle it before sunset, so as not to give the devil a foothold.

resolutions.name: Anger as a duty against evil
resolutions.heldBy: Some ethicists and social-justice readings; Lactantius wrote *On the Anger of God*
resolutions.explanation: Failing to be angry at cruelty can itself be moral failure. The command is a genuine instruction to be angry at the right things, with the right aim.

resolutions.name: Better to drop it
resolutions.heldBy: Desert Fathers and many monastic writers (e.g. John Cassian, *Institutes* book 8)
resolutions.explanation: Because human anger is almost always mixed with pride, the safest path is to root it out. Some early manuscripts of Matt 5:22 add 'without cause', which shaped this debate; most modern critical editions omit it.

skeptic.objection: Ephesians 4 says both 'be angry' and 'put away all anger' within six verses. That is incoherent.
skeptic.reply: Paul quotes a psalm to concede that anger arises, then sets limits so it does not become sin. Verse 31 lists anger with bitterness, slander and malice, the settled hostile kind. Scripture also attributes anger to God and to Jesus, so it cannot mean all anger is evil. The two verses form a single teaching: feel it, deal with it, don't keep it.

practical: When angry, ask what it is about: injustice to others or wounded pride? Address it before the day ends, by honest conversation or prayer. Don't let it settle into resentment.

title: Rejoice always, and weep with those who weep
plain: Paul says to rejoice in the Lord always, and in the same breath he describes himself as sorrowful yet always rejoicing. Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb, and Paul tells believers to weep with those who weep. Christians are called to joy and to grief at once.
takeaway: Christian joy is not the absence of sorrow but a hope that runs underneath it.

poleA.label: Rejoice
poleA.statement: Rejoice in the Lord always; count trials as joy; rejoice with joy inexpressible.

poleB.label: Weep
poleB.statement: Jesus wept; blessed are those who mourn; weep with those who weep; Paul had great sorrow and unceasing anguish.

tension: If joy is commanded 'always', is grief a failure of faith? If grief is right, how can joy be constant?

resolutions.name: Joy beneath sorrow
resolutions.heldBy: Most pastoral theology
resolutions.explanation: Joy in Scripture is rooted in God and hope, not in circumstances. It can coexist with sorrow like a deep current under a stormy surface. Paul calls himself 'sorrowful, yet always rejoicing'.

resolutions.name: Grief with hope
resolutions.heldBy: Readings of 1 Thessalonians 4
resolutions.explanation: Paul does not tell the bereaved not to grieve but not to grieve 'as others who have no hope'. Grief is real; hope changes its shape.

resolutions.name: A time for each
resolutions.heldBy: Wisdom tradition
resolutions.explanation: There is a time to weep and a time to laugh. Love matches the moment: rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Forcing cheerfulness on grieving people is unloving.

resolutions.name: Joy as a discipline
resolutions.heldBy: Many evangelical and charismatic devotional writers
resolutions.explanation: 'Rejoice' is an imperative: a choice to give thanks and praise God even in hardship, which then shapes feeling over time. Critics warn this can slide into denying pain.

skeptic.objection: Commanding people to rejoice always encourages toxic positivity and makes grieving believers feel guilty.
skeptic.reply: That is a real pastoral danger, but the Bible itself guards against it: it includes laments (about a third of the Psalms), shows Jesus weeping and troubled, and commands weeping with mourners. The 'always' of joy refers to a hope in God that is not cancelled by sorrow, not to a mood. Communities that suppress grief are departing from Scripture, not following it.

practical: Let yourself and others grieve honestly; read a lament psalm aloud. Look for small, real reasons for thanks even in hard seasons, without forcing them on someone else.

title: The kingdom is here, the kingdom is coming
plain: Jesus announced that the kingdom of God had come near, and even that it had arrived among people when he drove out demons. Yet he taught his followers to pray 'your kingdom come' and spoke of a future day when it would come in full. The kingdom is both present and future.
takeaway: God's reign has truly begun in Jesus but is not yet complete; Christians live in between.

poleA.label: Present
poleA.statement: The kingdom has come near, is in your midst, has come upon you; believers have been transferred into it.

poleB.label: Future
poleB.statement: Pray 'your kingdom come'; the Son of Man will come in glory; then comes the end when he hands over the kingdom.

tension: If the kingdom is here, why is the world still so broken? If it is future, what did Jesus' arrival change?

resolutions.name: Inaugurated eschatology ('already and not yet')
resolutions.heldBy: Most modern scholars across traditions (associated with George Ladd, Oscar Cullmann, and others)
resolutions.explanation: The kingdom was launched in Jesus' ministry, death and resurrection but awaits completion at his return. Cullmann compared it to a decisive battle already won while fighting continues until final victory day.

resolutions.name: Realised eschatology
resolutions.heldBy: C. H. Dodd and some later scholars
resolutions.explanation: The emphasis falls on the present: in Jesus the kingdom has fully arrived, and future-sounding language describes its spiritual reality. Critics say this underplays clear future texts.

resolutions.name: Consistent (future) eschatology
resolutions.heldBy: Albert Schweitzer and scholars who see Jesus as an apocalyptic prophet
resolutions.explanation: Jesus expected an imminent, dramatic arrival of God's kingdom; sayings about present arrival are anticipations of that soon-coming event. Critics say this neglects the present-tense sayings.

resolutions.name: Kingdom through the church
resolutions.heldBy: Various: Augustine's *City of God* (in a nuanced way), some postmillennial and dominion-oriented movements
resolutions.explanation: The kingdom grows now through the church's mission and influence until it fills the earth, like leaven in dough. Others reply that the final kingdom comes by God's act, not human progress.

skeptic.objection: Jesus predicted the kingdom would come within his hearers' lifetime; it didn't, so 'already and not yet' is a later patch for a failed prophecy.
skeptic.reply: This is a serious scholarly argument (Schweitzer and others). Responses include: texts like Mark 9:1 may refer to the transfiguration, resurrection or Pentecost; present-kingdom sayings show Jesus never held a purely future view; and Jesus also said no one knows the day or hour (Mark 13:32). Scholars remain divided, and readers should know the question is genuinely debated.

practical: Pray and work for signs of God's reign now (healing, justice, reconciliation) without expecting to perfect the world yourself. Hold hope for what only God can finish.

title: In the world, but not of it
plain: Jesus prayed not that his followers would be taken out of the world but that they would be kept from evil, since they are not of the world just as he is not. John says do not love the world, yet God so loved the world that he gave his Son. Christians are sent into a world they must not be shaped by.
takeaway: Christians are meant to be fully present in the world without being owned by its values.

poleA.label: In the world
poleA.statement: Jesus sends his followers into the world; they are salt and light; they seek the welfare of the city where they live.

poleB.label: Not of the world
poleB.statement: They are not of the world; do not be conformed to this age; do not love the world; friendship with the world is enmity with God.

tension: How close should Christians be to the surrounding culture? Withdrawal risks irrelevance; engagement risks compromise. And how can 'the world' be both loved by God and not to be loved?

resolutions.name: Two meanings of 'world'
resolutions.heldBy: Most interpreters of John's writings
resolutions.explanation: John uses *kosmos* both for humanity that God loves and for the system of life organised against God (pride, greed, lust). Love people in the world; refuse the world's way.

resolutions.name: Separation and distinct community
resolutions.heldBy: Anabaptist, monastic and some holiness traditions
resolutions.explanation: The church witnesses best as a visibly different community with its own practices, sometimes at a distance from political and cultural power.

resolutions.name: Transforming culture
resolutions.heldBy: Reformed tradition (e.g. Abraham Kuyper) and many Catholic social teaching writers
resolutions.explanation: Christians should enter every area of life, work, arts and politics, to bring it under Christ's lordship and seek the common good.

resolutions.name: Not leaving the world
resolutions.heldBy: Pauline readers
resolutions.explanation: Paul clarifies that avoiding immoral people does not mean avoiding non-Christians, 'since then you would need to go out of the world'. Holiness is about the church's own life, not about isolation.

skeptic.objection: The Bible says both 'God loves the world' and 'do not love the world', which is contradictory; and 'not of the world' breeds us-versus-them tribalism.
skeptic.reply: The word has two senses, as many words do; context separates them. On tribalism: the danger is real, but Jesus pairs 'not of the world' with being 'sent into the world', and Jeremiah tells exiles to seek the good of the very city that conquered them. The intended posture is distinct but engaged, not hostile.

practical: Ask where you are absorbing your culture's values without noticing (consumerism, outrage, status). Then ask where you are hiding from people who need your presence and help.

title: The meek inherit the earth, yet our citizenship is in heaven
plain: Jesus promised that the meek will inherit the earth. Paul says believers' citizenship is in heaven, and Hebrews calls them strangers and exiles seeking a homeland. So is the Christian hope earthly or heavenly?
takeaway: The biblical hope is heaven coming to a renewed earth, not escape from it.

poleA.label: Inherit the earth
poleA.statement: The meek shall inherit the earth; Abraham's offspring were promised the world; the redeemed will reign on the earth.

poleB.label: Citizens of heaven
poleB.statement: Our citizenship is in heaven; we seek a better, heavenly country; we have no lasting city here.

tension: If our home is heaven, why care about the earth? If we inherit the earth, what does heavenly citizenship mean?

resolutions.name: New heavens and new earth
resolutions.heldBy: Many contemporary scholars (e.g. N. T. Wright) and much Orthodox and Reformed theology
resolutions.explanation: Heaven is where God's rule is now; the final hope is the new Jerusalem coming down to a renewed earth. Paul's heavenly citizenship expects a Saviour coming 'from' heaven to transform the body, as Roman colonists in Philippi were citizens of Rome living elsewhere.

resolutions.name: Heavenly destiny
resolutions.heldBy: Much traditional Western piety and many popular evangelical readings
resolutions.explanation: The believer's true and final home is with God in heaven; 'the earth' is a figure for the blessings of God's kingdom. Present life is a pilgrimage.

resolutions.name: Land promise widened
resolutions.heldBy: Biblical-theological readings of Abraham's promise
resolutions.explanation: Psalm 37's promise of 'the land' to the meek is expanded in the New Testament to the whole world. Abraham was promised to be heir of the world.

resolutions.name: Millennial earthly reign
resolutions.heldBy: Premillennialists
resolutions.explanation: The saints will reign with Christ on this earth during a future millennium, before the eternal state; both earth and heaven feature in sequence.

skeptic.objection: Christianity can't decide whether its hope is pie in the sky or a political takeover of the earth.
skeptic.reply: The texts are not split between two incompatible hopes. Most traditions read them as one: God's heavenly reign comes to fill a renewed creation. Debates remain about timing and details (see the millennium debate), but the core picture of heaven and earth united is widely shared.

practical: Care for the earth and your neighbourhood as things God means to renew, not discard. Hold possessions and nationality loosely because your deepest loyalty is to God's kingdom.

title: Perfected for ever, yet being made holy
plain: Hebrews says that by one sacrifice Christ has perfected for all time those who are being made holy. Paul says he is not yet perfect and presses on, yet in the next breath addresses 'those who are perfect'. Believers are somehow complete already and still growing.
takeaway: In Christ believers are fully accepted now, and that secure standing is the ground for real growth.

poleA.label: Perfected
poleA.statement: By one offering Christ has perfected for ever those being sanctified; believers are complete in him and already washed and sanctified.

poleB.label: Being perfected
poleB.statement: Not that I am already perfect, but I press on; pursue the holiness without which no one will see the Lord; we are being transformed from glory to glory.

tension: If believers are already perfected, why must they strive? If they must strive, in what sense are they perfect? The answer shapes whether Christians live from security or for it.

resolutions.name: Definitive and progressive sanctification
resolutions.heldBy: Reformed and many evangelical theologians
resolutions.explanation: Hebrews speaks of believers' standing: the sacrifice has fully cleansed their conscience and qualified them to approach God. Growth in actual holiness is a lifelong process flowing from that settled standing. One is a status, the other a process.

resolutions.name: Infused grace that grows
resolutions.heldBy: Catholic teaching (Council of Trent, Session 6, on justification and its increase)
resolutions.explanation: Grace truly makes the believer righteous at baptism, and this righteousness can and should increase through cooperation with grace, the sacraments and good works. 'Perfected' refers to the sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice; the believer's share in it deepens.

resolutions.name: Christian perfection
resolutions.heldBy: Wesleyan and Holiness traditions
resolutions.explanation: John Wesley taught that believers may, by grace, reach a state of perfect love in this life, free from wilful sin though not from mistakes or growth. 'Perfect' in the New Testament often means mature and whole-hearted.

resolutions.name: Endless growth into God
resolutions.heldBy: Orthodox theology of *theosis*; Gregory of Nyssa (*Life of Moses*)
resolutions.explanation: Gregory of Nyssa argued that perfection itself is never-ending progress into God, since God is infinite. To be 'perfect' is to keep growing, even in the age to come.

skeptic.objection: Calling people 'perfect' who clearly aren't is either a legal fiction or a contradiction.
skeptic.reply: The word *teleios* means complete or brought to its goal, not flawless in behaviour. Hebrews' point is about access to God: what the old sacrifices could never do, Christ's has done once. Traditions do differ on whether this is a declared status (Protestant), an inner transformation (Catholic, Orthodox), or both, which is the real debate here, not a contradiction.

practical: Stop trying to earn the acceptance Christ has already secured, and stop using that acceptance as an excuse not to grow. Work on one habit or attitude out of security, not anxiety.

title: All things are lawful, but not all things help
plain: Twice in 1 Corinthians Paul writes 'All things are lawful' and immediately adds 'but not all things are helpful' and 'I will not be dominated by anything'. He affirms Christian freedom while limiting it. Many think 'all things are lawful' was a Corinthian slogan he is quoting.
takeaway: Freedom is real, but love and wisdom decide how to use it.

poleA.label: All things are lawful
poleA.statement: Believers are free from the Mosaic food laws and many religious scruples; nothing is unclean in itself.

poleB.label: Not all things help
poleB.statement: Not everything builds up; do not be mastered; do not let your freedom become a stumbling block; flee sexual immorality.

tension: If everything is permitted, why are some things forbidden? Does Paul really think 'all things', including immorality, are lawful?

resolutions.name: Corinthian slogan
resolutions.heldBy: Most modern commentators; many translations put the phrase in quotation marks
resolutions.explanation: Paul quotes a saying used in Corinth to justify behaviour (including using prostitutes, in chapter 6) and corrects it. He would agree in a limited sense, but not as they used it; the same chapter says the sexually immoral will not inherit the kingdom.

resolutions.name: Freedom in matters indifferent
resolutions.heldBy: Reformers and much Protestant ethics (*adiaphora*)
resolutions.explanation: 'All things' refers to matters not commanded or forbidden by God, like food offered to idols or holy days. In such matters believers are free, but they should choose what builds up others.

resolutions.name: Love limits liberty
resolutions.heldBy: Broad agreement across traditions
resolutions.explanation: Paul's test is not just 'Is it allowed?' but 'Does it help? Does it build up? Will it master me? Is it for God's glory?' Love for a weaker believer can mean giving up a right.

skeptic.objection: Paul says everything is lawful and then lists forbidden things. He wants it both ways.
skeptic.reply: Ancient letter writers often quoted an opponent's phrase and then qualified it, and the Corinthians had written Paul a letter with their own claims (1 Cor 7:1). Read as a quoted slogan, the passage is consistent: Paul accepts freedom from ritual law but not freedom from love and holiness.

practical: When deciding about a grey-area habit, ask four questions: Is it helpful? Does it control me? Does it build up others? Can I do it for God's glory?

title: How did Saul die?
plain: 1 Samuel 31 says the wounded Saul fell on his own sword after his armour-bearer refused to kill him. In the next chapter an Amalekite tells David that he himself killed Saul at Saul's request and brings Saul's crown as proof. The two stories sit side by side.
takeaway: Most readers see the narrator telling the truth and the Amalekite telling a self-serving lie, but there are other explanations.

poleA.label: Saul killed himself
poleA.statement: Badly wounded by archers, Saul asked his armour-bearer to kill him; when he refused, Saul fell on his sword.

poleB.label: The Amalekite killed him
poleB.statement: An Amalekite says he found Saul leaning on his spear, still alive, and killed him at his request, taking his crown and armlet to David.

tension: Both accounts appear in what was originally one continuous book (Samuel). Which is true, and why does the Bible include both?

resolutions.name: The Amalekite lied
resolutions.heldBy: Most traditional and many modern commentators
resolutions.explanation: The narrator reports Saul's suicide as fact; the Amalekite's version is reported speech from a man hoping for reward. He likely found the body, stripped it and invented a story. David later refers to him as one who thought he brought good news, and David had him executed.

resolutions.name: Both partly true
resolutions.heldBy: Some harmonisers; Josephus's retelling (*Antiquities* book 6) combines the two accounts in this way
resolutions.explanation: Saul's attempt failed to kill him outright; leaning on his spear, he asked the Amalekite to finish him. Critics note that 1 Samuel says the armour-bearer saw Saul was dead before killing himself.

resolutions.name: Literary characterisation
resolutions.heldBy: Literary critics of Hebrew narrative (e.g. Robert Alter)
resolutions.explanation: Hebrew narrative often reports a character's speech that differs from what the narrator has told us, to reveal motive. Here it shows the Amalekite's opportunism and highlights that David did not seize the throne by rejoicing in Saul's death.

resolutions.name: Two source traditions
resolutions.heldBy: Some historical-critical scholars
resolutions.explanation: The editor of Samuel combined two traditions about Saul's death, perhaps without fully reconciling them, or deliberately keeping both. Many critics nonetheless think the final text intends the reader to doubt the Amalekite.

skeptic.objection: The Bible gives two incompatible accounts of how Saul died, so it is historically unreliable.
skeptic.reply: Recording that a character lied is not the same as the text making contradictory claims. Only one account is given by the narrator; the other is a speech by a man with a motive, and the story treats him with suspicion. Harmonisation (he lied), literary explanations (characterisation) and critical explanations (two traditions) all exist; the first two remove the contradiction, and even the third does not show careless editing, since the passages are adjacent.

practical: Read Bible narrative carefully: not everything a character says is endorsed by the author. Notice how David refused to celebrate his rival's death.

title: Who incited David's census?
plain: 2 Samuel 24 says the Lord's anger burned against Israel and he incited David to count the people. 1 Chronicles 21, retelling the same event centuries later, says Satan stood against Israel and incited David. One text names God, the other Satan.
takeaway: The two accounts reflect different angles on how God's sovereignty and evil agents relate; how to read them is debated.

poleA.label: The LORD incited David
poleA.statement: The anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, 'Go, number Israel and Judah.'

poleB.label: Satan incited David
poleB.statement: Satan stood up against Israel and incited David to number Israel.

tension: Would God incite someone to sin and then punish it? And how can one account credit God and another Satan? (The accounts also differ in some numbers: e.g. 2 Sam 24:9 vs 1 Chr 21:5, seven vs three years of famine, and the price of the threshing floor.)

resolutions.name: God permits, Satan acts
resolutions.heldBy: Most traditional Jewish and Christian interpreters
resolutions.explanation: As in Job, God allows an adversary to test or provoke, using it for his purposes in judgment. Samuel names the ultimate cause, Chronicles the immediate agent. Both can be true at different levels.

resolutions.name: Double agency
resolutions.heldBy: Reformed and other theologians who stress providence
resolutions.explanation: Scripture often attributes one event to both God and human or evil agents, with different intentions: Joseph's brothers meant evil but God meant it for good; Jesus was crucified by lawless men according to God's plan.

resolutions.name: Theological development
resolutions.heldBy: Most critical scholars
resolutions.explanation: Chronicles was written after the exile, when Jewish thought increasingly attributed evil to an adversary figure rather than directly to God. The Chronicler reworked his source to avoid saying God incited sin. The Hebrew in 1 Chr 21:1 has 'satan' without the article, which may be a proper name or simply 'an adversary'.

resolutions.name: A human adversary
resolutions.heldBy: A minority of scholars
resolutions.explanation: Since *satan* can mean any adversary (it is used of human opponents), 1 Chr 21:1 might refer to a hostile foreign power or official whose threat provoked the census. This is possible but less widely held.

skeptic.objection: One book says God did it, the other says Satan. That is a direct contradiction, and the number differences prove the texts are unreliable.
skeptic.reply: On the inciter: harmonisers point to the Bible's repeated pattern of God working through evil agents (Job, 1 Kings 22), so both statements can be true at different levels. Critical scholars see a deliberate theological revision by the Chronicler, which is a change of emphasis rather than careless error. On the numbers: harmonisers suggest different counting bases (e.g. including or excluding certain groups) and scribal copying errors, which are common with numerals; critics see the Chronicler's own adjustments. Readers should know both explanations; neither side disputes that the Chronicler worked from Samuel.

practical: When bad things happen, the Bible neither makes God the author of evil in a simple way nor removes him from the picture. Hold God's sovereignty and human responsibility together, as David did when he confessed his own sin.

title: How did Judas die?
plain: Matthew says Judas threw the silver into the temple and went and hanged himself; the priests then bought a potter's field with the money. Acts says Judas acquired a field with the reward and, falling headlong, burst open. Both call the place the Field of Blood.
takeaway: Both accounts agree Judas died shamefully and that a field called Akeldama was linked to the money; they differ on details and on why it got its name.

poleA.label: Matthew: hanged himself
poleA.statement: Judas returned the money, hanged himself; the priests bought the potter's field, called the Field of Blood because blood money bought it.

poleB.label: Acts: fell and burst open
poleB.statement: Judas acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness; falling headlong he burst open, and it was called Akeldama, Field of Blood.

tension: Did Judas hang himself or fall? Did he buy the field or did the priests? Why was it called the Field of Blood: because of blood money or because of his blood?

resolutions.name: Hanging, then falling
resolutions.heldBy: Traditional harmonisation, widely held in conservative commentary
resolutions.explanation: Judas hanged himself; later the rope or branch gave way (or the body was cut down after decomposing) and it fell and burst. The priests bought the field with Judas's money, so it could be said he 'acquired' it through them. Both reasons for the name could be true.

resolutions.name: Different word sense
resolutions.heldBy: Some scholars
resolutions.explanation: The Greek *prenes genomenos*, usually 'falling headlong', may mean 'swelling up', which would fit a decomposing body and an early tradition (Papias, preserved by later writers) that Judas swelled grotesquely. This is debated.

resolutions.name: Scripture-shaped narratives
resolutions.heldBy: Literary and redaction critics
resolutions.explanation: Each writer shapes the story to fulfil Scripture. Matthew draws on Zechariah's thirty pieces thrown to the potter and Jeremiah's field purchase, and his hanging echoes Ahithophel, David's betrayer. Luke links the death to psalms about the wicked's dwelling being desolate. The theological framing explains the different emphases.

resolutions.name: Independent traditions
resolutions.heldBy: Many historical-critical scholars
resolutions.explanation: Early Christians knew Judas died badly and that a Jerusalem plot called Akeldama was linked with him, but separate traditions explained it differently. The accounts cannot be fully harmonised, and that is evidence the writers did not copy one another.

skeptic.objection: Matthew and Acts contradict each other on Judas's death, who bought the field and why it was named. Matthew even attributes a Zechariah prophecy to Jeremiah.
skeptic.reply: Harmonisers offer a plausible sequence (hanging then falling) and note that a purchase made with someone's money can be described as theirs. Literary readers note that each author frames the death through different Scriptures; Matthew's 'Jeremiah' may reflect a combined quotation, since the potter and a field purchase both appear in Jeremiah (Jer 18:1-4, Jer 32:6-9). Critical scholars accept that the accounts preserve different traditions. All agree on the core: Judas died soon, in disgrace, and the money was tied to a field known as the Field of Blood.

practical: Judas's end is a warning about despair as well as betrayal. Contrast Peter, who also failed Jesus but returned and was restored (John 21:15-17).
